newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa launches govt infrastructure funding firm.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa launches govt infrastructure funding firm.

text.p: A number of South African and offshore financial institutions have joined together to form a new finance company to help government fund its infrastructure needs, estimated at 171 billion rand over the next five years.

The Infrastructure Finance Corp Ltd (INCA), launched on Monday, intends to raise 12 billion rand over the next seven years in a move which sees the private sector joining government in addressing the country's massive infrastructure backlog.

At a press briefing on Monday INCA chairman Ismael Ayob said: "INCA is a direct response to an appeal made by government for private sector involvement in the provision of finance for infrastructure development."

Partners in INCA are First National Bank Holdings Ltd (FNB) and Southern Life Association Ltd each with a 20 percent stake, black-owned Msele Financial Holdings Ltd with 10 percent, the Women's Investment Portfolio with five, Old Mutual with 10, and the UK's Commonwealth Development Corp with 20 percent.
Negotiations with German investment and development company DEG on taking a 10 percent stake were at an advanced stage, as were talks on the final five percent.

INCA managing director Johan Kruger said funds would be raised through the issue of various capital market bonds, the first of which will be listed on the Bond Exchange of South Africa before the end of the year.
They were expected to raise around 1.2 billion rand in their first year of trade with FNB and Msele acting as market makers.

Funds would be used to provide five, 10 and 15 year debt financing at low rates of interest to all infrastructure providers, ranging from local authorities, water utilities and municipalities to private infrastructure companies, Kruger said. "The net cost of INCA finance to a borrower is directly derived from its own funding cost and the creditworthiness of the borrower," he said.

Creditworthiness would be measured by the application of a 55 point credit evaluation model which would consider, amongst other factors, the borrower's financial ability, economic growth prospects and socio-economic conditions.
INCA would initially be capitalised by a 50 million rand injection from its shareholders and a 44 million rand junior debt commitment, Kruger said.
